history.heading: Indigenous Taiwan and colonial rule
paragraphs: Taiwan, an island off the southeast coast of China, has been home to Austronesian indigenous peoples for thousands of years; linguists believe Taiwan may be the homeland from which Austronesian languages spread across the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

The Dutch established a colony in the south in 1624, and the Spanish briefly held the north. In 1662 Ming loyalist Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong) expelled the Dutch. The Qing dynasty took control in 1683, and Han Chinese immigration from Fujian and Guangdong grew. After the First Sino-Japanese War, Taiwan was ceded to Japan in 1895 and ruled as a colony for 50 years.

history.heading: Republic of China on Taiwan
paragraphs: In 1945 Taiwan was handed to the Republic of China (ROC). In 1947 an uprising against Nationalist rule was violently suppressed in the February 28 Incident. In 1949, after losing the Chinese Civil War to the Communists, Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist (Kuomintang) government retreated to Taiwan, along with about 1.5 million people.

Taiwan was ruled under martial law until 1987, a period known as the White Terror. The ROC lost its UN seat to the People's Republic of China in 1971. Taiwan democratised in the late 1980s and 1990s, holding its first direct presidential election in 1996, and has since had several peaceful transfers of power.

culture.heading: Language and culture
paragraphs: Mandarin is the main language, and Taiwanese Hokkien, Hakka and indigenous languages are also spoken. Religion is a mix of Buddhism, Taoism and folk religion, with temples such as Mazu temples central to community life. Taiwan was the first place in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage, in 2019.

Taiwan is famous for night markets and food such as beef noodle soup, xiaolongbao and bubble tea, which originated there. The National Palace Museum holds one of the world's greatest collections of Chinese art. Baseball is the most popular sport.

politics.heading: Democracy and status
paragraphs: Taiwan is governed as a democracy with a directly elected president and a legislature, the Legislative Yuan. The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), which emphasises a separate Taiwanese identity, and the Kuomintang (KMT), which favours closer ties with China, are the main parties. Lai Ching-te of the DPP became president in 2024.

The People's Republic of China claims Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out force to achieve unification; it conducts frequent military exercises near the island. Only about a dozen countries formally recognise Taiwan, though many, including the United States, maintain unofficial relations. Taiwan is not a UN member.

economy.heading: Semiconductor powerhouse
paragraphs: Taiwan has a high-income, export-oriented economy. It produces the majority of the world's most advanced semiconductors, led by TSMC, making it crucial to global technology supply chains, especially for artificial intelligence. Electronics, computers (Asus, Acer) and machinery are key exports.

Taiwan's economy grew strongly in 2024 and 2025 thanks to AI chip demand. Challenges include energy supply, an ageing population and dependence on trade with both China and the US. The currency is the New Taiwan dollar.
